reference.source: Walsh and Hoyt's Clinical Neuro-Ophthalmology / paediatric neurology literature
clinicalPearls: Episodes of sustained or intermittent conjugate upward deviation of the eyes, typically beginning in infancy
On attempted downgaze there are characteristic down-beating saccades while the eyes remain deviated upward
Attacks are often worse with fatigue and illness and may improve with sleep
Some children have associated ataxia or developmental and language difficulties
It is frequently benign and self-limiting, but structural and genetic causes must be considered
Associations with CACNA1A and other channel genes have been reported, overlapping with episodic neurological syndromes
reference.pathophysiology: Paroxysmal tonic upgaze reflects episodic dysfunction of the supranuclear control of vertical gaze, with a relative imbalance favouring upward deviation and impaired downgaze during attacks. Many cases are idiopathic and maturational, improving as the nervous system develops, while some are linked to channelopathies or to structural lesions of the midbrain and its vertical-gaze pathways. The down-beating saccades on attempted downgaze reflect preserved attempts to overcome the tonic upward drive.
additionalDifferentials: Structural midbrain lesion affecting vertical gaze
Spasmus nutans and other childhood eye-movement disorders
additionalInvestigations: MRI of the brain focusing on the midbrain and posterior fossa
Medication and metabolic review to exclude oculogyric crisis
Genetic evaluation where an episodic channelopathy is suspected
redFlags: Focal neurological signs or a structural lesion on imaging
Features suggesting seizures or oculogyric crisis
reference.prognosis: The idiopathic form usually improves over months to a few years, though some children have residual ataxia or cognitive and language difficulties; prognosis of secondary cases depends on the underlying cause.
pitfalls: Confusing it with drug-induced oculogyric crisis or seizures
Accepting a benign diagnosis without neuroimaging
Overlooking associated developmental or coordination problems
Missing an underlying channelopathy with broader implications
references: Taylor and Hoyt's Pediatric Ophthalmology and Strabismus
management: Manage idiopathic cases with reassurance and watchful observation, as most improve spontaneously with maturation
Consider a trial of levodopa, which has benefited some children in reported cases
Investigate and treat any identified structural midbrain lesion or metabolic cause underlying secondary presentations
Monitor development, language, and coordination, arranging early support for associated ataxia or learning difficulties
Pursue genetic evaluation and counselling where an episodic channelopathy such as CACNA1A is suspected
Follow up jointly through paediatric neurology and ophthalmology
